source_text:
Illum iam uelim conuenire, qui initiari nos dicit aut credit de caede infantis et sanguine. putas posse fieri, ut tam molle, tam paruulum corpus fata uulnerum capiat? ut quisquam illum rudem sanguinem nouelli et uixdum hominis caedat, fundat, exhauriat? nemo hoc potest credere nisi qui possit audere.
uos enim uideo procreatos filios nunc feris et auibus exponere, nunc adstrangulatos misero mortis genere elidere: sunt quae in ipsis uisceribus medicaminibus epotis originem futuri hominis extinguant et parricidium faciant, antequam pariant.
et haec utique de deorum uestrorum disciplina descendunt: nam Saturnus filios suos non exposuit, sed uorauit. merito ei in nonnullis Africae partibus a parentibus infantes immolabantur, blanditiis et osculo comprimente uagitum, ne flebilis hostia Îmmolaretur.
Tauris etiam Ponticis et Aegyptio Busiridi ritus fuit hospites immolare, et Mercurio Gallis humanas uel inhumanas uictimas caedere, Romanis Graecum et Graecam, Gallum et Gallam sacrificii loco uiuentes obruere, hodieque ab ipsis Latiaris Iuppiter homicidio colitur, et quod Saturni filio dignum est, mali et noxii hominis sanguine saginatur.
ipsam credo docnisse sanguinis foedere coniurare Catilinam, et Bellonam sacrum suum haustu humani cruoris imbuere, et comitialem morbum hominis sanguine, id est morbo graviore sanare.
non dissimiles et qui de harena feras deuorant inlitas et infectas cruore uel membris hominis et uiscere saginatas. nobis homicidium nec uidere fas nec audire, tantumque ab humano sanguine canemus, ut nec edulium pecorum in cibis sanguinem nouerimus.
thought_title: Christian innocence of infant blood and pagan blood-rites
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians are initiated by killing an infant and drinking its blood, and he turns the charge back onto pagan practices.
pass_a_gloss: That man I would now like to meet, who says or believes that we are initiated by the slaughter of an infant and by blood. Do you think it can happen, that so soft, so tiny a body receives the blows of wounds? That anyone should cut, pour out, drain that fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being? No one can believe this except one who could dare it. For I see that you expose your born children now to wild beasts and birds, now strangled, you crush them with a wretched kind of death: there are women who in their very wombs, by drinking drugs, extinguish the origin of a future human being and commit parricide before they give birth. And these things certainly descend from the teaching of your gods: for Saturn did not expose his sons, but devoured them. Deservedly to him in some parts of Africa infants were sacrificed by parents, with caresses and a kiss suppressing the wailing, so that a weeping victim might not be sacrificed. To the Taurians of Pontus and to Egyptian Busiris it was a rite to sacrifice guests, and to Gallic Mercury to slaughter human or inhuman victims, for the Romans to bury alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gaul and a Gaul woman in place of sacrifice, and even today by these very people Latiaris Jupiter is worshipped with homicide, and what is worthy of Saturn's son, he is fed with the blood of an evil and noxious man. I believe she herself taught Catiline to conspire by a covenant of blood, and Bellona to steep her sacred rite in a draught of human gore, and to heal the falling sickness with human blood, that is with a more serious disease. Not unlike are those who from the arena devour wild beasts smeared and stained with gore or with the limbs and entrails of a man and fattened. For us it is not lawful even to see or to hear of homicide, and so far do we keep away from human blood, that we do not even know the blood of slaughtered animals in our foods.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of fata as strokes or blows, not 'fate', since the context is physical wounding of an infant's body.

choices.term: rudem sanguinem nouelli et uixdum hominis
choices.english: the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being
choices.why: Renders rudem as 'fresh' for blood and nouelli as 'new', preserving the sense of a newborn not yet fully formed as a person.
rejected: the raw blood of a novice and hardly a man
the untrained blood of a new and barely human

choices.english: commit parricide before they give birth
choices.why: Keeps the paradox of parricide (killing one's own kin) applied to the unborn, and the temporal clause exactly.
rejected: commit murder before they bring forth
do a parent's murder before they bear

choices.english: so that a weeping victim might not be sacrificed
choices.why: Preserves the purpose clause and the adjective flebilis as 'weeping', matching the suppression of the infant's crying.
rejected: lest a lamentable victim be slain
so that a tearful sacrifice might not be offered

choices.why: Keeps the wordplay of humanas/inhumanas literally, since the Latin contrasts human victims with those treated as less than human.

choices.english: and so far do we keep away from human blood
choices.why: Renders canemus literally as 'we keep away from', preserving the verb of avoidance rather than a weaker 'abstain'.
rejected: and so much do we abstain from human blood
and we are so far from human blood

pass_b_english: Now I would like to meet the man who says or believes that we are initiated with the slaughter of an infant and with its blood. Do you think it possible that so soft, so tiny a body could receive the blows of wounds? That anyone could kill, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being? No one can believe this except one who could dare to do it.

For I see that you expose your own children to wild beasts and birds, or strangle them and crush them out with a wretched kind of death. There are women who, by drinking drugs, extinguish the origin of a future human being in their very womb, and commit parricide before they give birth.

And these practices certainly descend from the teaching of your gods: for Saturn did not expose his sons, but devoured them. Rightly were infants sacrificed to him by parents in some parts of Africa, with caresses and a kiss suppressing their crying, so that a weeping victim might not be sacrificed.

The Taurians of Pontus and the Egyptian king Busiris had the rite of sacrificing guests; the Gauls slaughtered human or inhuman victims to Mercury; the Romans crushed alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman, in place of sacrifice; and to this day Jupiter Latiaris is worshipped by them with homicide, and, what is worthy of Saturn's son, he is fed with the blood of a wicked and criminal man.

I believe this same superstition taught Catiline the practice of conspiring under a covenant of blood, and taught Bellona to steep her sacred rite in a draught of human gore, and how to cure epilepsy with human blood, that is, with a heavier disease.

Not unlike them are those who devour wild beasts from the arena, smeared and stained with blood or with the limbs and entrails of a human being. For us it is not lawful even to see or hear of homicide, and so far do we keep away from human blood that we do not even know the blood of animals among our food.

problems.why: Ipsam refers to Bellona (feminine), not Jupiter. Octavius says Bellona herself taught these things.
problems.ruling: ‘ipsam credo docuisse’ refers to a feminine antecedent (Bellona); translator used masculine ‘he’.

fixed: Changed 'he himself' to 'she herself' because ipsam is feminine and refers to Bellona, not Jupiter.

problems.quote: or crush them strangled by a wretched kind of death
problems.why: Latin says ‘to select’ the strangled victims, not to crush them; the English adds an action not in the source.
problems.fix: or select the strangled victims of a wretched kind of death

problems.why: The Latin refers to a common or epidemic disease, not specifically ‘the falling sickness’; the English introduces a specific disease not present.

edits.old: or crush them strangled by a wretched kind of death
edits.new: or strangle them and crush them out with a wretched kind of death

fixed: addition: 'or crush them strangled by a wretched kind of death' — source 'adstrangulatos misero mortis genere elidere' means 'strangled, to crush them out with a wretched kind of death'; 'elidere' does mean to crush out/destroy, so the English 'crush' is not an addition, but the participle 'adstrangulatos' was rendered as 'strangled by' instead of as a separate action. Fixed to 'or strangle them and crush them out with a wretched kind of death'.

mistranslation: 'the falling sickness' — source 'comitialem morbum' literally means 'the comitial disease' (a disease that interrupts assemblies, i.e. epilepsy), but the English 'falling sickness' is a specific English idiom for epilepsy. The source does not name epilepsy explicitly; 'comitialem morbum' is the Latin term for epilepsy. The English 'falling sickness' is a reasonable equivalent, but to stay closer to the source I changed it to 'the comitial disease'.

problems.quote: could strike, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being
problems.source_quote: qui illum rudem sanguinem nouelli et uixdum hominis caedat, fundat, exhauriat
problems.why: Latin verb caedat means ‘kill’, not ‘strike’; agency altered.
problems.fix: could kill, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a newly‑born, barely human being

problems.why: docuisse takes accusative+infinitive: 'taught that Catiline conspired' or 'showed Catiline conspiring'; not 'taught Catiline to conspire'.
problems.fix: showed Catiline conspiring by a covenant of blood
problems.ruling: coniurare Catilinam = conspire against Catiline; translation says “Catiline to conspire”, reversing roles.

problems.why: Third accusative+infinitive dependent on docuisse: 'and the curing of comitial disease...'; not 'taught men to cure'.
problems.fix: and the comitial disease being cured with human blood
problems.ruling: docuisse … sanare lacks “men”; adding “men” changes who is taught to cure.

problems.quote: the Romans buried alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman
problems.source_quote: Romanis Graecum et Graecam, Gallum et Gallam sacrificii loco uiuiens obruere
problems.why: Obruere means ‘crush/press down’, not ‘bury alive’; action misrepresented.
problems.fix: the Romans crushed alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman
problems.ruling: Obruere means 'crush/press down/overwhelm', not 'bury alive'; uiuentes modifies victims, but 'buried alive' misrepresents the killing method as burial rather than crushing/smothering.

edits.old: could strike, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being
edits.new: could kill, pour out, and drain the fresh blood of a new and scarcely yet human being

edits.old: taught Catiline to conspire under a covenant of blood
edits.new: showed Catiline conspiring under a covenant of blood

edits.old: and taught men to cure the comitial disease with human blood
edits.new: and the comitial disease being cured with human blood

edits.old: the Romans buried alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman
edits.new: the Romans crushed alive a Greek man and a Greek woman, a Gallic man and a Gallic woman

fixed: caedat means 'kill', not 'strike'; changed to 'could kill'.
docuisse takes accusative+infinitive; changed to 'showed Catiline conspiring'.
Third accusative+infinitive dependent on docuisse; changed to 'the comitial disease being cured'.
obruere means 'crush/press down', not 'bury alive'; changed to 'crushed alive'.

fixed.fix: this same superstition taught Catiline the practice of
fixed.note: Docuisse means 'taught', not 'showed', and 'she' has nothing to refer to; ipsam cannot be Bellona, who is the object of the next clause.

fixed.fix: how to cure the comitial disease
fixed.note: Sanare depends on docuisse ('taught ... how to cure'); the proposed fix would double the 'and' that comes before the quote.

dismissed.quote: or strangle them and crush them out with a wretched kind of death
dismissed.why: Latin has nunc...nunc (now...now), not 'or'; 'elidere' means to crush/kill, not 'crush them out'
dismissed.note: Rendering 'nunc...nunc' as 'or' is a fair choice, and 'crush them out' fits elidere.

polish.changed: Clarified that Busiris is an Egyptian king, identified the comitial disease as epilepsy, removed the em dash, and smoothed sentence flow while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: the Egyptian Busiris had the rite
notes.why: Busiris is a mythological Egyptian king associated with human sacrifice, unexplained.
notes.fix: Identify Busiris as a mythological Egyptian king known for sacrificing strangers.
Note: Busiris was a mythical Egyptian king who sacrificed strangers.

notes.quote: Jupiter Latiaris is worshipped by them with homicide
notes.why: Jupiter Latiaris and human sacrifice on the Mons Sacer are unexplained.
notes.fix: Note: Jupiter Latiaris was worshipped on the Alban Mount with human sacrifice.

notes.quote: Bellona to steep her sacred rite in a draught of human gore, and how to cure the comitial disease with human blood
notes.why: Bellona's rites and the comitial disease are unexplained.
notes.fix: Note: Bellona was a war goddess; comitial disease was epilepsy.

notes.quote: and how to cure the comitial disease with human blood—that is, with a heavier disease.
notes.why: 'Comitial disease' is unexplained and the parenthetical is unclear.
notes.fix: Note: comitial disease = epilepsy; 'heavier disease' = blood is worse than the disease.
